name: Civil 3D
tagline: Autodesk's civil-infrastructure design platform — alignments, profiles, corridors, surfaces, parcels, pipe networks, and pressure networks built on a DWG core.
meta_desc: Civil 3D profile: alignments and profiles, corridors, surfaces, pipe and pressure networks, plus 16 deep-dive terms and 16 FAQs reviewed by Gstarcademy editors.
first_released: 2006 (as Autodesk Civil 3D 2006); roots in Land Desktop and Autodesk Survey
current_track: Annual release — Civil 3D 2025; included in the AEC Collection
license_model: Subscription via Autodesk AEC Collection (typical) or single-product subscription (rare).

profile.what_it_is:
Civil 3D is Autodesk's specialised civil-engineering platform built on the AutoCAD DWG core. It adds civil-aware objects — surfaces (DEMs / TIN), alignments (horizontal centrelines), profiles (vertical centrelines), corridors (parametric road geometry derived from alignments + profiles + assemblies), parcels (subdivision lots), pipe and pressure networks (sewer / storm / water mains), and grading.

Civil 3D objects are intelligent: edit an alignment and every dependent profile, corridor, sheet, and quantity-takeoff updates. The platform produces both 2D plan-and-profile sheets and 3D models suitable for machine-control export.
profile.where_used: Civil 3D is the dominant civil tool in North America for roads, highways, subdivisions, and site-development design. State DOTs in the US, MTO in Ontario, and most large civil consultancies use Civil 3D as their primary design platform. Pipe and pressure networks are widely used for storm/sewer/water mains; rail and transit use Civil 3D less commonly than Bentley OpenRail.
profile.learning_curve:
Civil 3D has a famously steep learning curve. Coming from AutoCAD, the surface/alignment/profile/corridor object model is unintuitive. Coming from Bentley, the styles system feels indirect. Real productivity in design typically takes 3-6 months; sheet production another month; corridor modelling for complex urban projects another 3-6 months.

The consistent hardest concept is **styles**. Almost every Civil 3D object's appearance is controlled by a hierarchical styles system: object style, label style, code-set style for corridors, table style for parcels. Without a curated styles library, every drawing looks different and every fix is hand-applied.
profile.licensing_reality: Civil 3D ships only through Autodesk subscription, almost always as part of the AEC Collection (also includes Revit, AutoCAD, Navisworks, InfraWorks, ReCap). Single-product subscriptions exist but are usually less cost-effective. Education licenses are free with annual renewal.
profile.ecosystem:
Civil 3D extends via Subassembly Composer (visual programming for corridor assembly subassemblies), AutoCAD .NET API + COM, AutoCAD Map 3D shared object model (GIS interop), and AutoLISP. Notable add-ons: AutoTURN (vehicle swept paths), Streamline (drainage), Civil Site Design, and Subscriber Advantage Pack extensions.

For coordination, Civil 3D models export via Civil 3D Data Shortcuts (.xml) for project-team sharing and via LandXML for cross-platform exchange. InfraWorks consumes Civil 3D models for visualisation and conceptual analysis.
profile.common_pitfalls:
**Working without data shortcuts.** A drawing-by-drawing approach instead of central reference data leads to coordination nightmares.

**Custom styles per drawing.** Every drawing starts from a template; without enforcement, styles fragment across projects.

**Corridor over-targeting.** Targets that reference long-range geometry recompute slowly and break on minor edits.

**Surface explosion.** Importing a 50M-point lidar dataset as a TIN without simplifying — drawings become unusable.

**Pipe network labelling without a clear style.** Manual label edits get overwritten on next regenerate.
profile.when_to_use_vs_alternative:
Use Civil 3D for North American road and site-development work, where the DWG-based deliverable is contract-mandated and clients accept Civil 3D outputs.

Choose Bentley OpenRoads / OpenSite for projects with Bentley-mandated standards (many international transport agencies, some US DOTs). Choose 12d Model for Australia/NZ road work where it dominates. Choose Trimble TBC + Quantm for survey-and-design-as-built workflows tightly coupled to Trimble field hardware.

recommended_learning_path.focus: Civil 3D workspace, [points & point groups](./point-groups-civil-3d), [surfaces](./surfaces-civil-3d) from points, contours, slope analysis.
[Alignments](./alignments-civil-3d), [profiles](./profiles-civil-3d) (existing ground + design), profile view styles, profile labels.
[Grading](./grading-civil-3d), feature lines, slopes, daylighting, [parcels](./parcels-civil-3d), legal description.
[Pipe networks](./pipe-networks-civil-3d), [pressure networks](./pressure-networks-civil-3d), parts list, hydraulic calculations, sheet production.
[Data shortcuts](./data-shortcuts-civil-3d), reference templates, plan & profile sheets, machine-control export (XML), Subassembly Composer.

terms.title: Alignments (Civil 3D)
terms.short_def: Horizontal centrelines for roads, railways, and other linear infrastructure — composed of tangents, curves, and spirals.
terms.definition:
An alignment is a 2D path on the surface with stationing applied along its length. Civil 3D supports tangent-curve (with or without spirals) and free / fixed / floating constraints for entities. Alignments serve as the reference axis for profiles, corridors, pipe network parts, and sheets.

Design-criteria files enforce design rules (AASHTO, TAC, country-specific) flagging violations of minimum radius / superelevation / curve-length.
terms.why_matters: The alignment is the design's spine. Every downstream object — profile, corridor, sheet, pipe network — references it. Changing an alignment cascades correctly only if those references are intact.
common_pitfalls: Editing a tangent length without checking the connected free-curve recalculation — produces unexpected radii.
Defining alignments by polyline and converting — loses the constraint-based intelligence.
Skipping design criteria — design violates code silently.

quiz.question: When working with Alignments (Civil 3D), which of the following represents a common technical pitfall?
options: Editing a tangent length without checking the connected free-curve recalculation — produces unexpected radii.
Failing to manually re-index the SQL server database.
Over-allocating virtual memory caches in the cloud settings.
Restricting linetype scales strictly to 1:1 paper coordinates.
quiz.explanation: Correct. A common pitfall is 'Editing a tangent length without checking the connected free-curve recalculation — produces unexpected radii.' As the editorial review notes: 'The alignment is the design's spine. Every downstream object — profile, corridor, sheet, pipe network — references it. Changing an alignment cascades correctly only if those references are intact.'

terms.title: Profiles (Civil 3D)
terms.short_def: Vertical alignment of an alignment — existing ground profile and design profile in a profile view.
terms.definition:
A profile is a 2D path in elevation along an alignment. Existing-ground profile is sampled from a surface. Design profile is drawn or computed and contains tangents, curves (parabolic vertical curves), and grade breaks. Profile views display the profile graphically with stationing on the X-axis and elevation on the Y-axis.

Design criteria for profiles enforce K-value, minimum / maximum grades, sag/crest vertical curve length, sight distance.
terms.why_matters: The vertical profile is the road's grade design. It controls drainage, structures (bridges, culverts), and constructability.
common_pitfalls: Sampling an existing ground profile after the surface has been updated — labels stale.
Forgetting to break the profile at structure crossings — design grade doesn't match structure thickness.
Vertical curves that meet minimum sight distance but violate site lines through approaches.

terms.title: Corridors (Civil 3D)
terms.short_def: 3D parametric models of linear infrastructure — pavement, subbase, kerbs, sidewalks, shoulders, ditches — generated from alignment + profile + assemblies.
terms.definition:
A corridor combines a baseline (alignment + profile), an assembly (cross-section template), and regions (stations where the assembly applies). The corridor produces 3D surfaces (top, datum, etc.), feature lines (string lines along the corridor), and quantity-takeoff data.

Targets let subassemblies reference external geometry (offset alignments, ditch profiles, daylighting surfaces) for adaptive width and slope.
terms.why_matters: The corridor is the deliverable for road design — sheets, quantities, and machine-control models all derive from it. A well-built corridor regenerates cleanly on design changes; a poorly-built one requires hours of repair after every edit.
common_pitfalls: Single very-long regions instead of breaking at intersections / shoulder transitions.
Targets referencing alignments that change frequently — corridor regenerates slowly.
Frequency too high (one cross-section per metre on a 10 km corridor) — drawing becomes unusable.

quiz.question: When working with Corridors (Civil 3D), which of the following represents a common technical pitfall?
options: Single very-long regions instead of breaking at intersections / shoulder transitions.

quiz.explanation: Correct. A common pitfall is 'Single very-long regions instead of breaking at intersections / shoulder transitions.' As the editorial review notes: 'The corridor is the deliverable for road design — sheets, quantities, and machine-control models all derive from it. A well-built corridor regenerates cleanly on design changes; a poorly-built one requires hours of repair after every edit.'

terms.title: Assemblies (Civil 3D)
terms.short_def: Reusable cross-section templates composed of subassemblies — used by corridors to generate 3D geometry along an alignment.
terms.definition: An assembly is a 2D cross-section drawn at a station (or anywhere — it's a template). It has a baseline marker (where the alignment intersects in section) and contains subassemblies arranged on left/right sides. Each subassembly is a parametric piece (Lane, Curb, Sidewalk, Shoulder, Daylight). Corridors apply the assembly at each frequency station.
terms.why_matters: The assembly defines the road's cross-section. Standardised assemblies for each road class (Local, Collector, Arterial) produce consistent corridor output across a project.
common_pitfalls: Mixing custom subassemblies with stock — output styles inconsistent.
Subassembly parameters set to hard values when they should be alignment-driven.
Symmetric assemblies that should be asymmetric (e.g., kerbed one side, ditched the other).

quiz.question: When working with Assemblies (Civil 3D), which of the following represents a common technical pitfall?
options: Mixing custom subassemblies with stock — output styles inconsistent.
Failing to manually re-index the SQL server database.

quiz.explanation: Correct. A common pitfall is 'Mixing custom subassemblies with stock — output styles inconsistent.' As the editorial review notes: 'The assembly defines the road's cross-section. Standardised assemblies for each road class (Local, Collector, Arterial) produce consistent corridor output across a project.'

terms.title: Subassemblies (Civil 3D)
terms.short_def: Parametric building blocks of a cross-section — Lane, Kerb, Sidewalk, Shoulder, Daylight, etc., scripted in Subassembly Composer.
terms.definition: Subassemblies are AutoLISP/.NET coded geometry generators with parameters (lane width, slope, sub-base depth, kerb type). They attach at a connection point and emit links and points labelled by code. Civil 3D ships with the Subassembly Catalog (corridor stock library); Subassembly Composer authors custom subassemblies visually.
terms.why_matters: Subassemblies are the rules that produce road geometry. Custom subassemblies encode local design standards (DOT-specific kerb types, drainage profiles).
common_pitfalls: Authoring subassemblies that don't expose useful parameters — corridor needs surgery for each variation.
Forgetting to assign codes consistently — code-set styles fail to colour the right surfaces.
Recursive parametric loops in custom subassemblies — corridor generation hangs.

terms.title: Surfaces (Civil 3D)
terms.short_def: TIN (triangulated irregular network) or grid surfaces representing terrain, design grade, or any continuous Z-elevated surface.
terms.definition:
Surfaces in Civil 3D are TIN-based (or grid-based for very large datasets). They accept multiple data sources: point groups, point files, breaklines (linear features that force triangulation along them), boundaries (outer / hide / show / data clip), contour data, and DEM grids. Surface styles control display: contours, slope arrows, hillshade, watershed.

Surface analysis: slope, slope-arrows, watersheds, contour, water drop, volume calculation between surfaces.
terms.why_matters: Surfaces represent existing ground and design surfaces. Quantity calculations, profile sampling, corridor daylighting, and grading all depend on surface integrity.
common_pitfalls: Building a surface without breaklines on edge-of-pavement — incorrect triangulation across the road.
Importing a lidar dataset with millions of points — surface becomes unusable; should be simplified or gridded.
Mixing units in surface data — surface elevation is feet but contour interval set to metres.

terms.title: Point Groups (Civil 3D)
terms.short_def: Named filters that group survey/design points by description, number range, elevation range, or other criteria.
terms.definition: Point groups dynamically include points matching their query (e.g., 'all points with raw description matching CL*'). Display is controlled by the group's point style and label style. Surfaces accept point groups as data — adding new matching points to the group adds them to the surface automatically.
terms.why_matters: Without point groups, managing thousands of survey points is impossible. Point groups also drive which points are included in which surface.
common_pitfalls: Overlapping point groups with conflicting display styles — points flicker between symbols.
Hardcoding point ranges instead of using descriptions — adding new points doesn't auto-include.
Forgetting to update the source point group after a re-survey — surface still uses old data.

quiz.question: When working with Point Groups (Civil 3D), which of the following represents a common technical pitfall?

Over-allocating virtual memory caches in the cloud settings.

quiz.explanation: Correct. A common pitfall is 'Overlapping point groups with conflicting display styles — points flicker between symbols.' As the editorial review notes: 'Without point groups, managing thousands of survey points is impossible. Point groups also drive which points are included in which surface.'

terms.title: Grading (Civil 3D)
terms.short_def: Civil 3D's site-grading toolset — feature lines, grading objects, daylighting to target surface.
terms.definition:
Grading starts with a baseline (feature line, alignment, or polyline) and projects geometry at a defined slope/elevation/distance. Grading criteria specify the projection (e.g., 3:1 slope to target surface). Multiple grading criteria chain to produce embankments, ditches, lot grading.

Feature lines are 3D polylines with stations and elevations at each PI; they can be projected, smoothed, and intersected.
terms.why_matters: Site grading produces the design surface — graded pads, parking lots, ditches, embankments. Without grading discipline, sites don't drain correctly and don't tie cleanly to existing topography.
common_pitfalls: Grading objects without setting target surface — daylighting silently fails.
Mixing grading objects with manually edited feature lines — design surface has gaps.
Forgetting to add the grading output to the design surface — labels and contours don't update.

quiz.question: When working with Grading (Civil 3D), which of the following represents a common technical pitfall?

quiz.explanation: Correct. A common pitfall is 'Grading objects without setting target surface — daylighting silently fails.' As the editorial review notes: 'Site grading produces the design surface — graded pads, parking lots, ditches, embankments. Without grading discipline, sites don't drain correctly and don't tie cleanly to existing topography.'

terms.title: Parcels (Civil 3D)
terms.short_def: Boundary-based subdivision lots with area, perimeter, and legal description — used in land development and right-of-way design.
terms.definition:
A parcel is a closed boundary on the design plane with an associated parcel style, area label, segment labels (bearing/distance), and table entries. Parcels nest into a site, and editing one parcel boundary triggers neighbour parcel updates.

Legal description (metes and bounds) is generated from the parcel boundary geometry with templates for province/state-specific conventions.
terms.why_matters: For subdivision and land development, parcels are the deliverable. The plat sheet shows them by number with bearings, distances, and area.
common_pitfalls: Parcel boundary segments that should be curves modelled as polyline chord — area is off.
Parcels in different sites that should share boundaries — gaps between lots.
Forgetting to refresh labels after edit — labels show stale bearings.

quiz.question: When working with Parcels (Civil 3D), which of the following represents a common technical pitfall?

terms.title: Pipe Networks (Civil 3D)
terms.short_def: Gravity sewer and storm drainage networks — structures (manholes, catch basins) and pipes connected with inverts, slopes, and labels.
terms.definition:
Pipe networks define gravity flow: structures (manhole, catch basin, headwall, junction) at vertices and pipes between them. Each part comes from the parts list — manufacturers' catalogs. Rules govern minimum cover, minimum slope, drop at structures.

Networks display in plan, profile view, and section. Hydraulic analysis (SSA — Storm and Sanitary Analysis) consumes the network for capacity calculations.
terms.why_matters: Sewer / storm design is part of every site-development project. Civil 3D pipe networks integrate the routing, the labelling, and the hydraulic analysis in one model.
common_pitfalls: Switching parts lists mid-project — pipe sizes don't match the new parts.
Pipes that connect to structures at the wrong invert — water flows uphill in the analysis.
Manual label overrides — get overwritten on next regenerate.

quiz.question: When working with Pipe Networks (Civil 3D), which of the following represents a common technical pitfall?

quiz.explanation: Correct. A common pitfall is 'Switching parts lists mid-project — pipe sizes don't match the new parts.' As the editorial review notes: 'Sewer / storm design is part of every site-development project. Civil 3D pipe networks integrate the routing, the labelling, and the hydraulic analysis in one model.'

terms.title: Pressure Networks (Civil 3D)
terms.short_def: Pressurised water-main networks — fittings (elbows, tees, valves) connected with pipes, with depth and clash detection support.
terms.definition:
Pressure networks (added in Civil 3D 2013) model water distribution: fittings (elbow, tee, cross, valve, fire hydrant), appurtenances, and pipes. Routing uses 2D polyline-style layout, then depth is set per-section. Pressure pipes follow vertical and horizontal deflections within manufacturer-specified joint angles.

Clash detection between pressure networks and other infrastructure is built in.
terms.why_matters: Water distribution design needs separate handling from gravity flow. Pressure networks support the routing geometry, joint angles, fittings, and the depth constraints typical of water main work.
common_pitfalls: Routing without checking joint angles — pipes can't physically connect.
Wrong parts list — pipe diameters and fitting types don't match local AWWA / WQ standards.
Forgetting hydrant lateral lines — design omits required connections.

quiz.question: When working with Pressure Networks (Civil 3D), which of the following represents a common technical pitfall?

Failing to manually re-index the SQL server database.

quiz.explanation: Correct. A common pitfall is 'Routing without checking joint angles — pipes can't physically connect.' As the editorial review notes: 'Water distribution design needs separate handling from gravity flow. Pressure networks support the routing geometry, joint angles, fittings, and the depth constraints typical of water main work.'

terms.title: Data Shortcuts (Civil 3D)
terms.short_def: Shared references to Civil 3D objects (surfaces, alignments, profiles, pipe networks) across multiple drawings — the project-team coordination mechanism.
terms.definition: Data Shortcuts live in a shared project folder. One drawing 'publishes' an object (e.g., the design alignment); other drawings 'consume' it as a reference. Edits in the source flag the consumers for update on next open / save. Vault Civil 3D adds version control and check-in/check-out on top of the same model.
terms.why_matters: Civil 3D projects routinely involve 50+ drawings (plan, profile, cross-section, detail sheets). Data Shortcuts eliminate the need to duplicate geometry across them.
common_pitfalls: Working drawings outside the project's shortcuts folder — references can't resolve.
Publishing the same object from two drawings — ambiguous source.
Renaming the source drawing without going through Data Shortcut Manager — references break silently.

terms.title: Labels & Label Styles (Civil 3D)
terms.short_def: Civil 3D's parametric annotation system — alignment-station labels, profile labels, pipe labels, surface contour labels, all driven by named styles.
terms.definition:
Every Civil 3D object emits labels driven by its label style. The label style composes a series of content components (text, line, block, arrow) referencing object properties (Station, Elevation, Northing, Easting, Pipe Diameter, Invert). Edits to the style propagate to every label using it.

Label sets group multiple labels (e.g., a profile label set including station equation, grade break, sag curve crest).
terms.why_matters: Sheet production lives or dies by label style discipline. Without curated label styles, every drawing's labels look ad hoc.
common_pitfalls: Overriding label position by drag — gets reset on regenerate unless saved to the style.
Mixing US Survey Feet and International Feet on labels — micro-discrepancies accumulate.
Building labels with hardcoded text instead of expressions — labels lose accuracy when geometry changes.

terms.title: Machine Control Export (Civil 3D)
terms.short_def: Exporting corridor and surface models to machine-control formats — XML for Trimble / Topcon / Leica grading equipment.
terms.definition: Civil 3D exports models for use by grader / dozer / paver machine control systems. Common formats: LandXML (industry-standard), Trimble TILOS / Trimble Business Center XML, manufacturer-specific formats via Subscriber-Advantage extensions. The exported model includes the design surface, alignments, and station-elevation breaklines.
terms.why_matters: Machine control replaces stake-and-grade-checker workflows in modern earthworks. The accuracy of the export determines grade accuracy in the field.
common_pitfalls: Exporting a corridor before its surface has been built — exported model is incomplete.
Mismatched datum between design and field GPS — entire model is offset.
Forgetting to include breaklines — graders find smooth interpolation between sparse points.

terms.title: LandXML (Civil 3D)
terms.short_def: Open XML schema for civil data — alignments, profiles, surfaces, parcels, pipe networks — used for cross-platform exchange.
terms.definition: LandXML is a vendor-neutral XML format used to exchange civil model data. Civil 3D, Bentley OpenRoads, 12d Model, Trimble TBC, and most civil tools read/write LandXML. Civil 3D exports via File > Export > LandXML and imports via Insert tab > LandXML. The format covers alignments, profiles, surfaces, parcels, point lists, pipe networks.
terms.why_matters: LandXML is how a Civil 3D model reaches Bentley, 12d, or Trimble TBC users. Quality depends on what objects are exported and the version of LandXML in use.
common_pitfalls: Exporting LandXML version 1.2 to a recipient who expects 2.0 — schema mismatch.
Surfaces with too many TINs in one export — files become multi-GB.
Pipe networks with custom parts not mapped to LandXML conventions — receiver imports as generic geometry.

terms.title: Intersection Design (Civil 3D)
terms.short_def: Civil 3D's tool-driven workflow for designing intersections — primary alignment, secondary alignments, returns, and corner-radius geometry.
terms.definition: Intersections are objects in Civil 3D that combine multiple alignments and their corridors at a crossing. The intersection wizard generates the corner geometry (returns), profile relationships, lane drops, and corridor regions for the intersection footprint. Standard turning templates (AASHTO, NACTO, country-specific) provide default geometry.
terms.why_matters: Intersections are where road geometry is most complex and most consequential for safety. Civil 3D's intersection object encapsulates the tangent-curve-tangent return logic so editing one corner cascades to the connected geometry.
common_pitfalls: Intersection assembled before alignments are stable — minor alignment edits require intersection rebuild.
Wrong design vehicle template — return radii are too tight for the actual traffic.
Multiple intersection corridors using inconsistent assemblies — pavement steps at the corner.

quiz.explanation: Correct. A common pitfall is 'Intersection assembled before alignments are stable — minor alignment edits require intersection rebuild.' faqs.question: Is Civil 3D included with AutoCAD?
faqs.answer: No — Civil 3D is a specialty vertical that includes AutoCAD as a base layer. Subscribing to Civil 3D gives you AutoCAD too. Subscribing to AutoCAD alone does not include Civil 3D objects.

faqs.question: Can Civil 3D objects be opened in plain AutoCAD?
faqs.answer: Partially. Civil 3D objects appear as proxy objects in AutoCAD without Civil 3D — they display but are not editable. Use Object Enabler (free download) to give plain AutoCAD viewers richer display. For full editability, the receiver needs Civil 3D.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an alignment and a polyline?
faqs.answer: A polyline is dumb 2D geometry. An alignment is a Civil 3D object with stationing, design criteria, label-aware geometry (tangent / curve / spiral), and dependent objects (profiles, corridors, sheets). Always convert polylines to alignments for any civil design intent.

faqs.question: How do I share a Civil 3D drawing with someone who has Civil 3D but doesn't have my templates?
faqs.answer: Either eTransmit (Application Menu > Publish > eTransmit) which packages the DWG with referenced support files, or use Reference Templates so the recipient can attach the same template. For object styles to display correctly, the recipient must have the same styles available.

faqs.question: Why is my corridor not generating?
faqs.answer: Common causes: missing assembly, baseline alignment or profile reference broken, target surface no longer exists, region station range outside alignment extents, or one subassembly in the assembly is producing an error. Open the corridor properties and check the Events tab for the specific error message.

faqs.question: How do I export an alignment to LandXML?
faqs.answer: Toolspace > Survey or Toolspace > Prospector right-click on the alignment > Export to LandXML. Or use the File > Export > LandXML menu to export multiple objects at once. Choose the LandXML version that matches the receiver's tool.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a feature line and a 3D polyline?
faqs.answer: A feature line is a Civil 3D object with stationable PIs, elevation interpolation, grading projection capability, and editable per-station elevations. A 3D polyline is dumb AutoCAD geometry with vertex elevations. Feature lines are far more powerful for civil design.

faqs.question: Can I convert a surface from one drawing to another without LandXML?
faqs.answer: Yes — Data Shortcuts (the recommended approach). Publish the surface as a data shortcut from the source drawing; reference it in the target drawing. For one-time copies without coordination, surface export to TIN file and import is an alternative.

faqs.question: How do I find pipe network rule violations?
faqs.answer: Open the pipe network properties > Rules tab. Rules include minimum cover, minimum slope, drop at structure, maximum velocity. Civil 3D flags violations in the drawing (red highlighting) and in the network Toolspace panel.

faqs.question: Why are my profile labels stale?
faqs.answer: Either the underlying alignment / surface changed without label refresh, or you've manually overridden label position and the regeneration reset it. Use Modify > Update Labels or right-click profile > Labels > Edit Label Group.

faqs.question: How do I add a custom subassembly?
faqs.answer: Use Subassembly Composer (free with Civil 3D) to build the subassembly visually, package as .pkt, then load via Tool Palettes > Add Subassembly. Custom subassemblies can also be coded in .NET (more complex but more powerful).

faqs.question: What is the workflow for sheet production?
faqs.answer: Create a sheet set in AutoCAD Sheet Set Manager, link to data shortcuts. Build plan/profile/section template DWG files with viewports tied to alignments and stations. Civil 3D's Plan Production tools generate sheet runs automatically along alignments — one sheet per alignment chunk.

faqs.question: Why is my surface so large?
faqs.answer: Usually too many surface data points. Use surface boundaries (hide / data clip) to remove unnecessary area; simplify (Surface Properties > Simplify) to reduce TIN density; remove unused breaklines. For lidar data, consider a grid surface or convert outside Civil 3D first.

faqs.question: Can Civil 3D do BIM coordination with Revit?
faqs.answer: Yes — Civil 3D exports its design surfaces and alignments to Revit via the Civil 3D > Revit interoperability tools or via DWG / LandXML. Revit links them as references. For Roads-on-Bridges projects, the InfraWorks bridge module is the integration point between alignment design and structural design.

faqs.question: Is Civil 3D available on macOS?
faqs.answer: No. Civil 3D is Windows-only. Mac users typically use Parallels or Boot Camp (Intel Macs). Apple Silicon Mac users have very limited options for running Civil 3D natively.

faqs.question: Where do I learn Civil 3D systematically?
faqs.answer: Autodesk's Civil 3D Learning Path on learn.autodesk.com is the structured starting point. Tony Cabrera (Cabrera Engineering Consultants) and Mark Kiker (BeyondCAD blog) are practical authorities. For corridors specifically, the official Subassembly Composer documentation and the AECC corridor-design tutorial DWG are the canonical examples.
